name: Pack Vole
description:
The Pack Vole appears individually unremarkable — a stout, brown-grey rodent of roughly 20–25 cm body length with an unusually broad, flat skull, small rounded ears, and dense water-resistant fur. What distinguishes the species is not morphology but behavior: Pack Voles have evolved an extraordinarily rigid eusocial hunting and foraging system more reminiscent of social insects than mammals. A mature colony of 200–500 individuals operates with near-total coordination, moving through an environment in coordinated sweeps that can strip a food source — a waste dump, a storage room, a recently dead large animal — with startling speed. The broad skull houses an enlarged olfactory bulb and, uniquely, enlarged anterior cingulate cortex structures that researchers at Helix Biosystems documented in 2178 as producing unusually synchronized low-band neural oscillation across proximate colony members.

The Pack Vole's hunting behavior is its most alarming trait. While a single vole presents no meaningful threat to an adult human, a colony in full sweep mode will not divert around obstacles larger than themselves, including living animals or humans, unless physically repelled. They do not attack large animals strategically — they simply do not register them as a reason to stop moving. A person caught in a Pack Vole sweep in an enclosed space will experience hundreds of small bites from animals that are not acting aggressively but simply moving through. The sweeps are triggered by specific chemical signals from scout individuals and last 15–40 minutes before the colony disperses back to nest structures. They den in collapsed sub-floors, rubble fill, and the cavities beneath old concrete foundations.

Pack Voles are one of the genuinely feared vermin species in GLMZ's lower districts, not because of any individual animal's danger but because of the sweep phenomenon. In buildings with known colony presence, residents develop early-warning systems — usually other animals that react to the chemical signal the scouts release before a sweep begins. Dogs are commonly kept for this purpose. In a few neighborhoods, the Pack Voles have become so established that building layouts have been informally reorganized over generations to avoid den sites, creating strange architectural detours that newcomers find baffling until someone explains the carpet biters.
diet: Omnivore — grain, organic waste, insects, carrion, any protein source encountered during sweeps
notable_traits: Synchronized neural oscillation across colony members
No threat-avoidance response toward large animals during sweeps
encounters: The first sign of a sweep is often other animals reacting — dogs barking, cats fleeing, Razor Rats scattering from walls. The sweep itself arrives as a sound of scratching and the sensation of small bodies moving across floors, walls, and occasionally over humans if they don't move. In the open, a sweep can be sidestepped. In enclosed spaces, it cannot. Sweeps last 15–40 minutes.
known_uses: Dogs trained to detect the Pack Vole scout-signal are valued in Tier 1 housing (Φ 80–200 for a trained animal). No food or material use — the bites they leave are ragged and prone to infection.
story_hooks: A tenant organizer trying to document unsafe housing conditions in a Tier 1 block gets caught in a Pack Vole sweep during a basement inspection and has to be treated for dozens of small bite wounds — someone locked the basement door from the outside just before the sweep started

A Helix Biosystems researcher's 2178 study on Pack Vole neural synchronization has recently been cited in a patent application for a new crowd-control technology — and the researcher has been missing for three months
